name: Seasilver

lead: Seasilver was a liquid dietary supplement made by Seasilver USA and Americaloe of Carlsbad, California, and sold through distributors. It combined aloe vera, a plant-based silver ingredient, sea vegetables, pau d'arco, cranberry concentrate and vitamins and minerals. Its marketing promised broad health benefits, including weight loss.

For appearance purposes, the relevant claim was weight loss without dieting. In 2003 the FTC and FDA said the product's cure claims were false and unsubstantiated, and the companies settled in 2004. Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center has stated that no studies demonstrated its effectiveness.

paras: It was sold as a liquid supplement in 32-ounce bottles at about 39.95 US dollars, taken by the serving as directed on the label and recommended to customers by network marketing distributors.

The main documented harm was financial and informational: customers were sold a product on the basis of claims regulators found unsupported, including claims that it could replace diabetes medication. The product was discontinued after the legal actions.

angle.text: Distributors marketed it for general health, including weight loss without dieting. Regulators found the claims unsubstantiated, and it is no longer sold.

lead: Seasilver was a liquid dietary supplement sold through network marketing by Seasilver USA, Inc. (founded 1992) and Americaloe, Inc., both of Carlsbad, California. Its ingredients included aloe vera, a silver ingredient described as plant-based phytosilver, sea vegetables, pau d'arco and cranberry concentrate. A 32-ounce bottle cost 39.95 US dollars [1][2].

Its relevance to looks lay in its marketing as a general wellness and weight-loss product. The FTC alleged in 2003 that promoters claimed it was clinically proven to treat or cure 650 diseases, including cancer and AIDS, and that it caused rapid, permanent weight loss without dieting [1].

No published studies of Seasilver have been identified; Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center states that none demonstrated effectiveness [2]. The product and companies are mainly remembered for the enforcement action.
infobox: FDA warning letter 2002; FTC/FDA action June 2003; settlement March 2004 [1][2]

paras: Seasilver was sold through distributors, and before legal action the companies reportedly claimed 180 million dollars in annual profits [2]. A 2003 post on T Nation shows a user whose friend 'swears by it' asking whether it was worth the price, which a user in another thread noted was shut down for claiming to cure diseases [3][4].

The FDA sent a warning letter in 2002 over claims touching blood sugar, allergies, arthritis, heart disease and cancer risk [2]. In June 2003 the FTC and FDA announced coordinated action; the FTC's complaint named the two companies, principals Bela and Jason Berkes, and distributors Brett Rademacher and David Friedman. It alleged claims that Seasilver treats or cures cancer, lets nine in ten diabetes patients stop insulin, and causes permanent weight loss without dieting [1].

Final orders were entered on 4 March 2004 in the US District Court in Nevada. They set a 4.5 million dollar total redress, a 120 million dollar judgment against the companies and Berkes suspended on payment of 3 million, bans on unsupported health claims, and FDA-ordered destruction of 5.3 million dollars of misbranded product. The settlements did not admit violation of law [1]. FTC consumer protection director Howard Beales said that products touted as cure-alls almost always cure nothing [1].
In June 2006 a federal judge upheld the full 120 million dollar penalty after the companies paid under a third of the refund amount, and the Ninth Circuit reaffirmed it on 10 April 2008 [2].
